title: Pathways: buying more first jobs
prompt: Our client is a national Ministry of Labour. Its flagship youth programme, Pathways, spends $300M a year training unemployed young people, but a spending review has challenged the ministry to show results. A two-year pilot of an alternative model — classroom training combined with paid employer apprenticeships — has just reported. The minister must decide whether to keep the current model or move Pathways to the apprenticeship model, and has asked us to look at the evidence.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 1 — Pathways today: the classroom model
exhibits.unitsNote: A placement means a participant in work six months after finishing

exhibits.title: Exhibit 2 — The apprenticeship pilot
exhibits.unitsNote: Measured on the same placement definition as Exhibit 1

rows: Benefits no longer paid, per placement

questions.prompt: Before we compare the two models, what should we clarify with the ministry first? Select the two most relevant.
options: What is the programme actually trying to maximise — participants trained, or people in work?
Is the budget fixed, or does the ministry expect to spend more or less?
Which building the programme’s administrators sit in?
What the minister studied at university?
The font used in the programme’s brochures?

optionRationale: The objective decides the answer: the two models rank differently on throughput than on jobs.
The constraint. Comparing models only makes sense at a defined budget — and a spending review means it will not grow.
commonMistakes: Assuming the metric is participants served, when the review is about outcomes
Comparing the models at different budgets without noticing

questions.followUp:
The objective is employment: the review measures Pathways on people in work six months after the programme, not on seats filled. Today the programme trains 50,000 participants a year.

And the budget is fixed at $300M — the comparison is what each model delivers for the same money.

Here is the current model.

questions.prompt: Which areas would you examine to make the recommendation? Select the four most relevant.
options: Cost per placement under each model — what a job actually costs to create
What the fixed budget delivers under each model — placements, and participants served
Whether the pilot’s results would survive scaling to the whole country
The wider fiscal effect — benefits saved when someone moves into work
The ministers who ran the programme in the 1990s
The catering arrangements at training centres

optionRationale: The core efficiency measure, and the one the spending review will quote.
The budget is fixed, so the real question is what $300M buys — and the models trade off participants against placements.
The classic pilot trap: small pilots get the most motivated employers and participants; scale may dilute both.
Placements pay back twice — once in wages, once in benefits not paid. The review will want that number.
commonMistakes: Stopping at cost-per-placement and missing the participants-served trade-off, which is where the political difficulty lives
Taking pilot results as guaranteed at national scale

questions.followUp: Here are the pilot results, measured on the same definitions as the current programme.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, what does one placement — one young person in work — cost under the current model?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in dollars, rounded to the nearest dollar.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Participants: $300M ÷ $6,000 = 50,000 a year.
Placements: 50,000 × 40% = 20,000.
Cost per placement: $300M ÷ 20,000 = $15,000. (Or directly: $6,000 ÷ 0.40.)
commonMistakes: Quoting the $6,000 cost per participant as the cost per placement
Dividing by participants instead of placements

questions.followUp: So each job costs $15,000 — because the ministry pays for the 60% of participants who do not end up in work as well. Now the same figure for the pilot model.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, what does one placement cost under the apprenticeship model?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in dollars, rounded to the nearest dollar — for $12,500, type 12500.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Cost per placement: $8,000 ÷ 0.60 ≈ $13,333.
More expensive per participant, cheaper per job.
commonMistakes: Concluding the model is worse because $8,000 > $6,000 — the placement rate more than compensates
Multiplying by the placement rate instead of dividing

questions.followUp: That is the pivot of the case: the apprenticeship model costs a third more per participant but over 10% less per job. The next question is what that means at the programme’s actual budget.

questions.prompt: If the whole $300M moved to the apprenticeship model, how many placements would Pathways deliver a year?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter the number of placements, rounded to the nearest hundred.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Participants: $300M ÷ $8,000 = 37,500 a year.
Placements: 37,500 × 60% = 22,500 — against 20,000 today.
commonMistakes: Keeping 50,000 participants at the new cost, which overspends the budget by $100M
Applying the 60% rate to today’s 50,000 participants

questions.followUp:
2,500 more young people in work each year from the same money. The trade-off: participants served falls by 12,500, from 50,000 to 37,500 — fewer places, better odds. Both facts belong in the minister’s brief.

One more number: the fiscal side.

questions.prompt: Each placement saves the government $4,000 a year in benefits no longer paid. How much extra does the apprenticeship model save the treasury each year, versus the current model?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in $ millions, rounded to the nearest million.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Extra placements: 22,500 − 20,000 = 2,500 a year.
Extra saving: 2,500 × $4,000 = $10M a year.
commonMistakes: Applying the $4,000 to all 22,500 placements instead of the incremental 2,500
Treating the saving as one-off when it recurs for as long as the person stays in work

questions.followUp: So the switch pays a dividend beyond the programme: $10M a year back to the treasury, on top of more young people in work. What should still give the minister pause is the next question.

questions.prompt: What are the most relevant risks in moving Pathways to the apprenticeship model? Select the three most relevant.
options: Scale risk — the pilot may have attracted the most willing employers, and 37,500 apprenticeships need many more
Selection risk — the pilot may have enrolled more motivated participants, flattering the 60% rate
Equity risk — 12,500 fewer places a year, and it matters who loses them
Currency risk on the programme’s budget
The risk that classroom buildings fall empty

optionRationale: The central scaling question: employer demand for apprentices is the model’s raw material, and pilots recruit the easy supply first.
The classic evaluation trap: if the pilot’s participants were unusually motivated, the national rate lands below 60%.
Real and political: a model that helps fewer people more is a defensible choice, but only if made openly and with care for who is excluded.
A domestic programme in domestic currency.
A managed transition handles facilities; it is not a decision-level risk.
commonMistakes: Reading pilot numbers as national numbers
Treating the drop in participants served as a footnote rather than a decision the minister must own

questions.followUp:
Scale: phase the transition region by region, and recruit employers ahead of participants.

Selection: keep the independent evaluation running through the rollout, with results measured on the full intake.

Equity: use part of the treasury saving to protect places for the hardest-to-reach participants, who benefit most from the programme even at lower placement rates.

questions.prompt: The minister has ten minutes before the spending-review hearing and asks for your recommendation. Please give your answer in seven to eight lines maximum.

keyPoints: Leads with the recommendation: move Pathways to the apprenticeship model, phased
Gives the outcome numbers: 22,500 placements a year versus 20,000, at $13,333 per job versus $15,000, on the same $300M
Adds the fiscal dividend: $10M a year of benefits no longer paid
Owns the trade-off honestly: 12,500 fewer places a year — states it rather than hiding it
Names the conditions: region-by-region rollout, continued independent evaluation, and protected places for the hardest to reach
Stays inside seven or eight lines
commonMistakes: Hiding the drop in participants served, which the hearing will find anyway
Presenting pilot results as guaranteed at national scale
Leading with the fiscal saving rather than the employment outcome the programme exists for

closing: That is the end of the case. Your transcript is ready — copy it into an LLM to be graded on what you actually said, not on what you meant.
